articles.title: UN upholds housing as a human right on World Habitat Day
articles.summary: Representatives from governments, civil society and academia meeting in Muscat, Oman on Monday called for urgent action to address a global housing crisis affecting nearly 3.4 billion people.
articles.content:
They gathered to commemorate World Habitat Day which this year focuses on the theme of Adequate Housing for All.

“Adequate housing is not a luxury. It is a foundation for a dignified life and for sustainable cities,” said Anacláudia Rossbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat, the agency that promotes sustainable urbanization.

Tweet URL

She stressed that “housing needs to be treated as a public priority alongside land and basic services”, underlining the need for greater investment in communities and cooperation across government, the private sector and civil society.

Millions living in slums

In his message for the day, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called adequate housing for all “the foundation of dignity, security, and opportunity.”

He noted, however, that more than three billion people worldwide are denied this universal human right.

“Over one billion live in informal settlements and slums, and many more experience homelessness or have been displaced by conflict, disasters, and climate change,” he added.

Trapped in poverty

The President of the United Nations Habitat Assembly, Nga Kor Ming, reminded participants that behind the numbers are real people.

Mr. Ming – Malaysia’s Minister of Housing and Local Government – highlighted the plight of families living in homes without legal protection, or even basic sanitation and clean water, whose children suffer preventable diseases.

“A house without clean water, safety or legal security is not a home. It is a poverty trap,” he said in a video message. “Therefore, to deliver adequate housing for all, we must move away from quick fixes to systemic transformation.”

More than four walls

Ms. Rossbach explained that under the UN human rights framework, housing is considered adequate when it meets seven criteria that include availability of services, habitability, affordability, location and accessibility.

“Adequate housing means much more than a physical structure with four walls and a roof,” she said.

“A family may have a roof and still spend so much on rent that there is little left for food, education, or healthcare. A home may be affordable, but located far from jobs, schools, or transport.”

Soundcloud

Everyone at home

The UN Secretary-General upheld that “investing in adequate housing and transforming informal settlements reduces poverty, tackles inequality, builds climate resilience, and fosters peaceful and inclusive societies.”

He called for coordinated action by national and local governments, building stronger partnerships, and better use of data in decision-making.

“The international financial architecture must also be reformed to mobilize the adequate, predictable, and affordable financing developing countries need to invest in housing at scale,” he added.

The Secretary-General ended his message with an appeal to the international community.

“On this World Habitat Day, let us treat housing as a public good and build a world where everyone has a place to call home,” he said.

A month of action

World Habitat Day is observed annually on the first Monday in October.

It marks the start of UN-Habitat’s Urban October – a month-long campaign to advocate for housing and sustainable urban development that concludes on World Cities Day, 31 October.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

It emphasizes the broad societal impact of housing on dignity, security, poverty reduction, and sustainable development, with detailed context and a call for coordinated international efforts.
articles.personality_title: UN calls for urgent action on global housing crisis on World Habitat Day
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year on the first Monday of October, the United Nations (UN) marks World Habitat Day to focus attention on housing and sustainable cities. This year, the theme was "Adequate Housing for All," highlighting the serious problem that nearly 3.4 billion people worldwide lack proper homes.

**What happened** – On World Habitat Day, representatives from governments, civil society, and universities met in Muscat, Oman. They agreed that housing is a basic human right, not a luxury, and called for urgent action to fix the global housing crisis. UN leaders stressed that housing must be a public priority alongside land and essential services like water and sanitation.

**Impact** – This event is important because it underlines how many people live in unsafe and overcrowded places without legal protection or basic services. Over one billion live in slums or informal settlements, and many more are homeless or displaced by conflicts and climate change. Adequate housing means more than just a roof—it includes being affordable, safe, and close to jobs and schools. Without this, families can remain trapped in poverty and poor health.

**What's next step** – The UN is pushing for governments and private groups to work together and invest more in housing. They want better data to make smarter decisions and changes in how money is provided to poorer countries to build more affordable homes. The month of October is now a time for worldwide campaigns to promote lasting solutions to housing problems.

**One-sentence takeaway** – On World Habitat Day, the UN highlighted that safe, affordable, and legal housing is a basic right that requires urgent, coordinated global action to improve billions of lives.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU appelle à une action urgente face à la crise mondiale du logement lors de la Journée mondiale de l’habitat
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, le premier lundi d’octobre, l’Organisation des Nations Unies (ONU) célèbre la Journée mondiale de l’habitat pour attirer l’attention sur le logement et les villes durables. Cette année, le thème était « Un logement adéquat pour tous », soulignant que près de 3,4 milliards de personnes dans le monde n’ont pas de logement convenable.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lors de cette journée, des représentants des gouvernements, de la société civile et du monde universitaire se sont réunis à Mascate, Oman. Ils ont convenu que le logement est un droit humain fondamental, pas un luxe, et ont appelé à une action urgente pour résoudre la crise mondiale du logement. Les dirigeants de l’ONU ont insisté pour que le logement soit une priorité publique au même titre que la terre et les services essentiels comme l’eau et l’assainissement.

**Impact** – Cet événement est important car il montre combien de personnes vivent dans des lieux dangereux et surpeuplés, sans protection légale ni services de base. Plus d’un milliard vivent dans des bidonvilles ou des quartiers informels, et beaucoup sont sans abri ou déplacés par des conflits et le changement climatique. Un logement adéquat ne se résume pas à un toit : il doit être abordable, sûr et proche des emplois et des écoles. Sans cela, les familles restent prisonnières de la pauvreté et de la mauvaise santé.

**Prochaines étapes** – L’ONU encourage les gouvernements et les acteurs privés à coopérer et à investir davantage dans le logement. Elle demande de meilleures données pour prendre des décisions plus efficaces et des changements dans le financement pour aider les pays pauvres à construire plus de logements abordables. Le mois d’octobre est désormais consacré à des campagnes mondiales pour promouvoir des solutions durables.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Lors de la Journée mondiale de l’habitat, l’ONU a souligné que le logement sûr, abordable et légal est un droit fondamental nécessitant une action mondiale urgente et coordonnée pour améliorer la vie de milliards de personnes.
articles.personality_title_es: ONU pide acción urgente ante la crisis mundial de vivienda en el Día Mundial del Hábitat
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, el primer lunes de octubre, las Naciones Unidas (ONU) celebran el Día Mundial del Hábitat para llamar la atención sobre la vivienda y las ciudades sostenibles. Este año, el tema fue "Vivienda adecuada para todos", destacando que casi 3.4 mil millones de personas en el mundo no tienen un hogar adecuado.

**Qué sucedió** – En el Día Mundial del Hábitat, representantes de gobiernos, sociedad civil y universidades se reunieron en Mascate, Omán. Coincidieron en que la vivienda es un derecho humano básico, no un lujo, y pidieron acciones urgentes para resolver la crisis mundial de vivienda. Los líderes de la ONU enfatizaron que la vivienda debe ser una prioridad pública junto a la tierra y servicios esenciales como agua y saneamiento.

**Impacto** – Este evento es importante porque muestra cuántas personas viven en lugares inseguros y hacinados sin protección legal ni servicios básicos. Más de mil millones viven en barrios informales o asentamientos precarios, y muchos más están sin hogar o desplazados por conflictos y cambio climático. La vivienda adecuada es más que un techo: debe ser asequible, segura y cercana a empleos y escuelas. Sin esto, las familias quedan atrapadas en la pobreza y la mala salud.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU impulsa que gobiernos y sectores privados trabajen juntos e inviertan más en vivienda. Quieren mejores datos para tomar decisiones inteligentes y cambios en la financiación para que los países pobres puedan construir más hogares asequibles. Octubre es ahora un mes dedicado a campañas globales para promover soluciones duraderas.

**Resumen en una frase** – En el Día Mundial del Hábitat, la ONU destacó que una vivienda segura, asequible y legal es un derecho básico que requiere una acción global urgente y coordinada para mejorar la vida de miles de millones.

articles.title: When radio finds a new digital voice: Bringing Romani language and culture online in Kosovo
articles.summary: Digital transformation does not always require expensive infrastructure or complex solutions. For community media, it can begin by taking valuable content that already exists and giving it a longer life.
articles.content:
This article was produced by Durmish Aslano from Radio Romano Avazo through the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

For years, Radio Romano Avazo has been one of the few spaces where the Romani language and culture could be heard consistently in Kosovo. Broadcasting from Prizren, the community radio station has provided content for Roma audiences who often have limited access to media in their mother tongue.

But as media consumption increasingly moves online, one question became impossible to ignore: What happens to Romani-language content when the radio broadcast ends?

Through the “Romani Voice Digital: Podcast Platform for Civic Inclusion” project, Radio Romano Avazo took an important step toward answering that question by transforming its existing cultural content into podcasts, creating a digital presence for Romani-language audio on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, YouTube, and its website.

The project was more than just a technological upgrade. It was an attempt to fill a space that had been missing for the Roma community in Kosovo: A dedicated digital space where the Romani language, culture, stories, and voices could continue to exist and be accessed whenever and wherever people wanted.

From live radio to a permanent digital archive

Radio content traditionally depends on a specific moment. If listeners are not available when a program is broadcast, they can easily miss it. This limitation was particularly relevant for the station’s “Gjuha dhe Kultura” (Language and Culture) program, which contains conversations and stories that deserve to remain accessible beyond a single broadcast. This project changed that model.

Three key episodes were selected and adapted into a podcast format, allowing audiences to listen to them on demand. This was an important transition for a small community media outlet: From producing content that disappears after a broadcast to creating an accessible digital archive of Romani voices and cultural knowledge.

Three stories, three personalities, one language

At the heart of the project were conversations with three personalities who have each contributed to the Romani language, culture, and public life in different ways.

The first episode, “Skolatar ani Bibloteka” (From the Classroom to the Library), featured Urma Menekshe, a teacher of the Romani language in Prizren and the creator of the Roma Mini-Library. She is also an author and translator.

Her story connects education, books, and language preservation, showing that language doesn’t just occur through institutions, but unfolds within classrooms, libraries, family homes, and everyday conversations.

The second episode, “Artesta ani Politika” (From Art to Politics), brought the audience closer to Sejnur Veshall, a politician and former deputy minister in the Ministry of Culture, as well as an actor and poet.

His experience provided an opportunity to explore the relationship between culture and public life, while also discussing the challenges the Roma community faces and the importance of stronger support for Romani culture and language in Kosovo.

The third episode, “Kulturatar ani Televizia” (From Culture to Television), featured Daut Qulangjiu, editor of the Roma-language newsroom at RTK, as well as a former dancer, folklorist, and actor.

His personal journey brought together traditional culture, performance, media, and television, offering listeners a glimpse into how Roma cultural expression has evolved and how it can continue to find space in contemporary media.

One of the strengths of the podcasts was their human dimension.

The conversations were not limited to formal questions about language, culture, or professional achievements. Listeners were also able to discover the personalities behind the public roles.

This approach helped transform the episodes from conventional interviews into conversations that audiences could connect with.

At the same time, the guests were invited to share their views and recommendations on how the situation of the Roma community could be improved, particularly in relation to language and culture.

A digital space that the community was already waiting for

Perhaps the strongest indication of the project’s relevance came immediately after the content was published.

The podcasts were promoted through specially designed visual materials and shared through the communication channels already used by the Roma community. The response was unexpectedly strong.

Roma audiences not only from Prizren but also from other municipalities began asking how they could access the podcast episodes.

These questions were significant.

They showed that the challenge was not necessarily a lack of interest in digital content. Instead, there had been a lack of Romani-language content worth looking for.

The podcasts are also designed to reach beyond Kosovo. Since they are available on international platforms, Romani speakers in the diaspora — from Europe and beyond — can access stories and conversations in their own language.

For a community whose language crosses borders, this creates an opportunity to strengthen connections between Roma in Kosovo and Roma living elsewhere.

Measuring impact beyond numbers

The project set clear ambitions for audience growth, including more than 500 listens and more than 200 new followers, while also aiming to create a sustainable podcast section on the Radio Romano Avazo website.

The initial response already indicates significant interest, with the content reaching tens of thousands of views/listens across digital channels to date.

Yet the project's impact cannot be measured only through analytics.

Every new person who discovers a Romani-language podcast represents another opportunity for the language to be heard. Every person who shares an episode with a family member or friend contributes to its circulation. And every young Roma person who encounters their language and culture in a modern digital format is reminded that Romani also belongs in the digital world.

The experience demonstrates that digital transformation does not always require expensive infrastructure or complex solutions. For community media, it can begin by taking valuable content that already exists and giving it a longer life. The project also showed that there is an audience for Romani-language digital content.

The next challenge is sustainability.

The podcast section on the Radio Romano Avazo website can become a permanent home for future episodes, cultural conversations, and other Romani-language productions. The initial three podcasts can serve as a foundation for a larger digital archive and a broader strategy for engaging young people, women, rural Roma communities, and the wider Roma diaspora.

Most importantly, the project has demonstrated that language preservation and digital inclusion can go hand in hand.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful digital inclusion project that preserves and promotes the Romani language and culture in Kosovo by transforming radio content into accessible podcasts. This initiative supports cultural preservation, language rights, and community empowerment for a marginalized group, with broad significance for Roma communities locally and in the diaspora. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights tangible positive impacts on cultural access and digital inclusion.

articles.title: Rising numbers of Asian and African PhD students choose to study in China
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02798-6International students explain the advantages and challenges that come with pursuing a doctoral degree in China.
articles.content:
Engineering graduate students from Egypt, Yemen, Indonesia and Niger watch a demonstration of a smart construction system at Southeast University in Nanjing, China. Credit: Heng Jiang

Every weekday, Fatma Satyani, an Indonesian PhD student in China, gets up at 7.30 a.m. to get ready for her day.

She usually eats a youtiao (fried dough stick) or a couple of baozi (steamed buns) with warm soya milk, a traditional Chinese breakfast, before heading out to classes at the Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology in eastern China.

“I love studying here,” says Satyani, who is doing a PhD on big data and business intelligence. “Chinese people are friendly, the food is delicious and getting around Nanjing is very convenient.”

Satyani is one of a fast-growing group of students from low- and middle-income countries — especially nations in Asia and Africa where China has made large investments in development — who are seeking a postgraduate education in the Asian superpower.

The number of international university students in China has climbed steadily since the nation lifted its strict COVID-19 pandemic lockdown rules in late 2022. According to the latest official statistics reported by China Daily, a state-run newspaper, 380,000 international students were studying in the country during the 2024–25 academic year, up by 15% from the previous year. Even so, these students made up less than 1% of the 48.5 million students in China’s higher-education system in the 2024–25 academic year. And the proportion of international students in China represents just a fraction of the share studying in the United States and the United Kingdom (see ‘A small fraction’).

Sources: HESA; IIE; NCES; Ministry of Education of China; ChinaDaily

In China, 61% of international students come from Asia, with most of the rest coming from Africa and Europe, at 16% each. About 71,750 of those are in master’s or PhD programmes, according to statistics from the government. Although on the rise, the number of international students is still lower than China’s 2018 pre-pandemic record of nearly 500,000 students, according to QS Quacquarelli Symonds, a UK-based company that analyses global higher-education institutions.

On the move: why PhD students study abroad in 2025

International PhD students based in China say that they were attracted to the programmes by generous scholarships, the opportunity to learn Mandarin and make Chinese connections and China’s rising capabilities in frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence and data analytics. However, they also face several obstacles. Mandarin is a difficult language to master, and students often have limited options to stay in China after their courses end. Moreover, some countries consider a Chinese degree to be less competitive.

“In the past, we saw that America was the global first in science, technology and education. Looking ahead, I think China will be the global first in those areas, including attracting and training students and researchers from around the world,” Satyani says.

Learn from China

Satyani is in the second year of her PhD programme, having completed a two-year master’s in business management at the same university. She moved to China to study in 2023 because her university in Indonesia, Universal University in Batam, suggested that she do so after completing her bachelor’s degree there.

“I would like to work for Universal University as a professor in the future, so the university assisted me to come to China to study so that I can bring the knowledge I learn in China back to Indonesia and teach the students there,” Satyani says.

After her master’s, Satyani decided to pursue a PhD in China because she had enjoyed her life there and she “wanted to study something that would be useful for the future”. For her, China is a perfect place to learn how companies and governments use big data — large data sets that can be used to assess trends and patterns — and AI tools to improve efficiency. “You’ve got to learn futuristic knowledge in a futuristic country,” Satyani says.

Similarly, meteorology PhD student Aminu Dalhatu Datti was drawn to study at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology because, he says, it is a leading institution for meteorology and its advanced computing systems enable him to use complex models for data analysis. Datti, who is from Nigeria, says that he “had heard a lot of good things about China”, including the fact that it has a fast-growing economy and provides strong support for international students. “So, I wanted to come here and see the country with my own eyes.”

Chairina Hanum Siregar (third from left) introduced people to Indonesian tea and snacks at a cultural exchange event at Sichuan University in Chengdu, China, where she’s studying a PhD in management science.Credit: International Office of the School of Business, Sichuan University

Datti says that he’s been able to attend international meteorology conferences in China and that the knowledge and connections he’s gained from those will be valuable to him when he finishes his PhD and returns to his post at the Nigerian Meteorological Agency in Abuja.

For others, such as Chairina Hanum Siregar, it was lifestyle factors and scholarships that made China attractive. “As a woman, safety is very important, and I really like that the city of Chengdu is safe.” Siregar, who is from Jakarta, is a third-year PhD student in management science and engineering at Sichuan University in Chengdu.

Siregar also applied to universities in the United Kingdom and Australia but did not receive any scholarship offers. She says that she did not apply to universities in the United States at all because of concerns about public safety there.

Building soft power

In 2010, China launched a national campaign called Study in China to attract more global students and to “cultivate a batch of high-quality international students who understand China and are friendly to China”. In 2016, it announced that it would incorporate its international strategy for higher education into the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), its global infrastructure and development strategy. The initiative has projects in more than 140 partner countries, most of which are low- and middle-income nations. In a statement made at the time, the government described education and trade as the “two wings” that would propel the BRI forward.

All of the students interviewed by Nature’s careers team hold government scholarships. The exact level of sponsorship varies, but for a PhD student, the awards usually include tuition fees and medical insurance, as well as a monthly stipend and free or subsidized housing.

China’s generous scholarships play a key part in attracting international students, says Tu Mengwei, a sociologist at Swansea University, UK. For example, Satyani is a recipient of the Chinese Government Scholarship, which provides her with 3,500 yuan (around US$520) per month and free housing.

China’s effort to make its higher-education system more international has also involved strategies to attract post-PhD researchers from overseas, including people with Chinese ancestry, to work in China. “All of that is a part of a bigger scheme of expanding China’s soft power and global influence,” Tu says.

Changing demographics

“Although the total number of international students in China has bounced back since the pandemic, the demographics have changed dramatically,” says Wen Wen, a higher-education specialist at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

In 2018, South Korea was the largest source of international students in China, followed by Thailand, Pakistan, India and the United States, Chinese government figures show. But in 2024, the five nations sending the most students to China were Thailand, Pakistan, Vietnam, Russia and Indonesia, according to QS (see ‘China’s student sources are changing’).

Alice Wei, a consultant at QS, isn’t surprised. China has always been a popular destination for students from Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam because of the close political ties and frequent trade activity between the nations, Wei explains. The rapid economic growth of countries in southeast Asia has also driven a demand for talent, leading young people to seek a high-quality education abroad, she says.

Sources: Ministry of Education of China; QS Quacquarelli Symonds

In Tu’s view, the influx of international students from Pakistan and other BRI nations in 2018–23 — when she was doing field work on the experiences of international students in China1 — was not only driven by China’s targeted policy, but also the applicants’ own plans and desires. For example, as China has strengthened its transport and infrastructure links with Pakistan, students there “gradually discovered that they would have better job opportunities if they learn to speak Mandarin or have connections in China,” Tu notes. “It’s a two-way street.” China has been building the Pakistan Economic Corridor2 since 2015, a $62-billion flagship project under the BRI that aims to construct a series of transport and infrastructure facilities linking Pakistan’s Gwadar Port on the Arabian Sea to western China’s landlocked Xinjiang autonomous region.

By contrast, the number of South Korean and US students in China has dropped. According to data from South Korea’s education ministry, South Korean student numbers plummeted by nearly 80% between 2017 and 2023, and the number of students from the United States in China shrank from around 24,000 in 2017 to just 400 in 2023, according to QS. The large drops are mostly due to China’s strict lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tension and worsening public sentiment towards China in these nations, researchers say.

Dedicated programmes

International students in China mostly study dedicated, predominantly English-speaking courses set up by universities. Few students live, study or do research alongside their Chinese peers. China has a long tradition of managing international students separately from their Chinese counterparts owing to immigration and public-security rules, Wen says.
